query: Platinum-group metals can promote distinct reactions, and earlier PGM-based nanoscale catalysts showed strong activity, selectivity, and durability in complex catalysis. A representative catalyst was reported to perform particularly well in ethanol oxidation, which involves 12-electron and 12-proton transfers, but these performance reports did not establish a comprehensive causal explanation of its behavior during operation. Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs its catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Define an unnamed controlled change with a suitable baseline, the predicted observations, the reaction regime in which the hypothesis should apply or fail, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: The catalytic activity of Platinum-group metals (PGM) nanoscale catalysts in ethanol oxidation is governed by the synergistic effects between different metal sites, which regulate the binding strength of proton and hydroxyl, and therefore enhance the reaction rate.
generation.intervention: Introduction of high-entropy alloy (HEA) structure with multiple metal sites
generation.conditions: Ethanol oxidation reaction in complex catalysis
generation.structural_mediator: Synergistic effects between different metal sites
generation.mechanism: Regulation of binding strength of proton and hydroxyl
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability
generation.baseline: Conventional PGM catalysts without HEA structure
generation.boundary: Reaction conditions: temperature, pressure, and ethanol concentration
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of synergistic effects and the optimal composition of HEA structure

falsification_experiment.design: Comparison of catalytic activity between PGM catalysts with and without HEA structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the catalytic activity of PGM catalysts with HEA structure is not significantly higher than that of conventional PGM catalysts, the hypothesis is falsified. Threshold: 20% increase in reaction rate.

Herein, we report the synthesis of a class of hierarchical Pt-Co NWs enclosed with high-density high-index facts through a robust large-scalable wet-chemical approach as electrocatalysts for fuel cell reactions. Unlike conventional Pt-M NWs, these hierarchical Pt-Co NWs with highly uneven surfaces are tailored to have an ordered intermetallic structure, high-index facets and a Pt-rich surface, which can meet several critical design criteria for efficient nanoelectrocatalysts. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) with unique physicochemical properties have attracted tremendous attention in many fields, yet the precise control on dimension and morphology at atomic level remains formidable challenges. Herein, we synthesize unique PtRuNiCoFeMo HEA subnanometer nanowires (SNWs) for alkaline hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR). The mass and specific activities of HEA SNWs/C reach 6.75 A mgPt+Ru−1 and 8.96 mA cm−2, respectively, which are 2.8/2.6, 4.1/2.4, and 19.8/18.7 times higher than those of HEA NPs/C, commercial PtRu/C and Pt/C, respectively. It can even display enhanced resistance to CO poisoning during HOR in the presence of 1000 ppm CO. Density functional theory calculations reveal that the strong interactions between different metal sites in HEA SNWs can greatly regulate the binding strength of proton and hydroxyl, and therefore enhances the HOR activity. This work not only provides a viable synthetic route for the fabrication of Pt-based HEA subnano/nano materials, but also promotes the fundamental researches on catalysis and beyond. Recently, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted increasing attention in diverse fields due to their inherent properties, including high thermal stability, strong mechanical strength, excellent corrosion resistance, and fine trade-off effect on performance. As promising catalysts in heterogeneous catalysis, HEAs generally consist of five or more metals, which display the structure-dependent synergistic effects and enhanced catalytic performance in terms of activity and durability,. Moreover, since the HEAs can largely decrease the usage of noble metals and thus reduce the cost of catalyst, they have been attracted increasing research interests. For instance, Li et al. reported a small HEAs Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27 nanoparticles (NPs) with a mean size of ~3.4 nm as an efficient catalyst for alkaline methanol oxidation reaction, on which the synergistic effects facilitate the site-to-site electron transfer during both reduction and oxidation processes. Cui et al. demonstrated that the synergistic effects between different metals in CrMnFeCoNi HEA sulfide can regulate the electronic states and thus enhances the oxygen evolution reaction activity.
